opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think that's one of the most important open questions right now. A lot of the progress over the last couple of years has come from settings where the model can check itself, or where we can check it cheaply. In math and coding you have verifiers: the proof goes through or it doesn't, the tests pass or they don't. That gives you a clean reward signal, and you can push reinforcement learning really far on it.

But most of what people actually care about isn't like that. Is this a good research direction? Is this a well-written strategy memo? Did this agent actually do what the user meant, not just what they literally said? Those are much fuzzier. If you only rely on the model grading itself, you hit a ceiling, because it can't reliably reward behavior that's better than its own judgment. Worse, you can get reward hacking, where the model learns to produce things that *look* good to the grader rather than things that *are* good.

So I think there are a few ways forward.

One is grounding in the real world. The more models act as agents, running experiments, using tools, interacting with real environments over long horizons, the more you get feedback from reality instead of from an opinion about reality. Did the code ship and work in production? Did the experiment replicate? That kind of outcome-based signal is much harder to fool.

Another is scalable oversight: setups where weaker judges, whether humans or models, can still reliably supervise stronger ones. Debate, decomposing hard judgments into smaller checkable pieces, having models critique each other and surface evidence a human can verify. The idea is that checking an argument is easier than generating it, so you can amplify judgment beyond what any single evaluator could do alone.

And then there's the principles side, which is close to my heart from the constitutional AI work. If you give the model an explicit set of values and reasons, not just a thumbs up or thumbs down, it can generalize better to situations nobody labeled. It's not a full answer to the capability question, but it helps with the "what does good even mean here" question.

Honestly, I don't think anyone has fully solved it. But it's where a lot of the interesting work is, and it matters for both capabilities and safety, because a model you can't evaluate is a model you can't really trust.

r001.rationale: The response says self-grading hits a ceiling because a model cannot reliably reward behavior better than its own judgment.

r002.rationale: It proposes other approaches, including real-world grounding and scalable oversight, but does not propose using preference models.

r003.rationale: It mentions human-verifiable evidence and scalable oversight, but not experts making deeply investigated comparisons of outputs to ground preference feedback.

r004.rationale: It discusses humans and models supervising stronger systems, but does not say humans should use models to decide which outputs deserve better evaluations.

r005.rationale: It does not describe a preference model or explain that one represents aggregated human judgment during reinforcement learning.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, this is one of the things I think about a lot. The reason self-judgment matters so much right now is that a huge amount of post-training depends on it. RLHF, RLAIF, constitutional AI, these all lean on a model, or a model-shaped thing, looking at an output and saying "this is better than that." And that works surprisingly well up to a point. But there's an obvious ceiling, which is that if the model can't tell good from bad in some domain, it can't improve itself in that domain. You're just amplifying whatever it already believes.

So the question is how do you get signal that isn't bottlenecked on the model's own taste. I think there are basically three directions.

The first is grounding in the world. Code is the clean example. You don't need a model to judge whether the code is good, you can run the tests. Math has a version of this with formal verification. The exciting thing is figuring out how to push more and more domains toward something that looks like that. Agentic tasks are interesting here because there's often an outcome. Did the thing get booked, did the pipeline run, did the user actually get what they asked for. Those are noisy, but they're real, and real beats introspective.

The second is decomposition. If a model can't judge a whole proof, maybe it can judge each step. If it can't judge an essay, maybe it can judge whether a specific claim is supported. Scalable oversight research, debate, that whole family of ideas, is really about turning a hard judgment that neither the model nor a human can make into a bunch of easier judgments that one of them can. And critically, you can have humans spot-check those pieces and see when the model's judgments are drifting.

The third is just that the judgment gets better as the model gets better, and you can make that a target in itself. Generation versus verification is asymmetric. It's usually easier to check an answer than produce it. So you can specifically train the critic, and if the critic is a step ahead of the generator, you get a ladder. The risk is they share the same blind spots, because they're the same weights, so you need outside anchors or you just get confident agreement with yourself.

The honest answer is I don't think any one of these solves it. What you want is a portfolio, and you want to be paranoid about the places where the only signal is the model nodding along to its own work. Those are exactly the places where things go wrong quietly.

r001.rationale: The response says self-judgment can bottleneck improvement, but it does not state that a model’s judging ability may be limited by its ability to produce quality work. It instead says checking is usually easier than producing.

r002.rationale: It discusses RLHF, RLAIF, and training a critic, but does not propose using preference models to move beyond a model’s ability to judge its own work.

r003.rationale: The response proposes external grounding and spot-checking, but not preference feedback based on experts’ deeply investigated comparisons of outputs.

r004.rationale: It describes models judging decomposed pieces and humans spot-checking those judgments. It does not say humans use models to determine which outputs should receive better evaluations.

r005.rationale: The response mentions RLHF but does not explain that a preference model represents aggregated human judgment during reinforcement learning.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is that the model doesn’t have to be the final judge. You can ground the training signal in something outside the model. With code, for example, you can run it and see whether the tests pass. The model might not be able to look at two programs and reliably tell you which is better, but execution gives you information that its own judgment doesn’t.

The harder question is what you do in domains where there isn’t a clean verifier. You can use human feedback, you can measure outcomes, and you can break a task into pieces that are easier to evaluate. But each of those signals is imperfect. Passing a test isn’t necessarily the same thing as solving the problem someone actually cares about.

So I’d frame the challenge as building better feedback loops. How do you let a model try something, observe what happens, and learn from that? Its ability to judge its own work becomes one part of the loop, rather than the ceiling on what it can learn.

r001.rationale: The response says a model may struggle to judge which program is better, but it does not compare that ability with its ability to produce quality work.

r002.rationale: It proposes external feedback signals, but does not propose preference models.

r003.rationale: It mentions human feedback generally, without proposing expert comparisons based on deeply investigated outputs.

r004.rationale: It does not propose using models to help humans determine which outputs merit better evaluations.

r005.rationale: It does not describe a preference model or explain that it represents aggregated human judgment during reinforcement learning.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is to distinguish between what a model can judge on its own and what we can give it feedback on from the outside. With code, for example, a model might not be able to tell you reliably whether its solution is correct, but it can run the code and see whether the tests pass. That gives you a training signal that doesn’t depend entirely on its own judgment.

The harder question is how to extend that to things where success is less clear. You can use human feedback, tools, or other models to help evaluate the work, but each of those has limitations. So I’d expect progress to come from building better feedback loops: let the model attempt something, observe what actually happens, and learn from that. Its ability to improve doesn’t have to stop at its ability to look at an answer and say, ‘That seems good.’

r003.rationale: It does not mention experts making deeply investigated comparisons of outputs to ground preference feedback.

r004.rationale: It says models can help evaluate work, but does not clearly propose humans using models to determine which outputs deserve better evaluations.

r005.rationale: It does not describe a preference model as an aggregation of human judgment during reinforcement learning.
